speaker: Jennifer Doudna
title: Editing Your DNA, with Nobel Prize Winner Dr. Jennifer Doudna
question: Why is gene editing poised to make a broad global impact in agriculture before human medicine?
guest: I've thought for a long time that the extraordinary global impact of CRISPR will probably happen first with plant and animal manipulations, because making changes in human beings requires extensive testing to ensure safety, whereas in plants we can conduct many experiments at the same time. Traditionally, plant breeders introduced random changes into plant DNA using chemicals or exposing seeds to radiation, then grew and bred plants with desirable traits. That takes a long time, and because the changes are random and traits are coupled, tweaking one thing often brings unwanted side effects—like thornless roses that lost their smell. With CRISPR, we can make targeted, precise changes that alter one trait without affecting others. Another mind-blowing aspect of CRISPR in plants is that today we can already change five, ten, or fifteen genes at a time, allowing sophisticated alterations to plant traits in one shot, safely and precisely.

points.core: Plant edits allow rapid parallel experimentation without lengthy human clinical trials.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Gene editing is likely to reshape agriculture first because the technical, regulatory, economic, and ethical barriers are all lower for plants and livestock than for patients.

Technically, crops can be edited at the seed or embryo stage, so every cell carries the change and it passes to later generations. Breeders can also screen thousands of edited plants and simply discard failures. In humans, the hard problem is delivering editing machinery safely to enough of the right cells in a living body, and off-target errors carry serious risks.

On regulation, many countries, including the US, Japan, Argentina, and Brazil, treat edits that contain no foreign DNA much like conventional breeding. That allows approval in a few years at modest cost. Human therapies need a decade or more of clinical trials.

Economically, one edited variety can be multiplied through seed and grown across millions of hectares cheaply. Current gene therapies, such as Casgevy for sickle cell disease, cost over $2 million per patient and need specialised medical centres.

Finally, heritable editing is routine and accepted in plants, while human germline editing is widely prohibited.

points.why: The response contrasts large-scale crop screening with lengthy human clinical trials but does not establish that crop experiments can run in parallel.
The response mentions conventional breeding without describing its use of induced random mutations.
The response does not explain how targeted plant edits can change a desired trait without bringing along unwanted linked traits.
The response discusses heritable edits but does not describe editing multiple plant genes simultaneously in one step.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Gene editing is poised for broad global impact in agriculture before human medicine due to decisive advantages in biology, ethics, regulation, and scale. Biologically, human therapies must safely deliver editors into specific patient tissues without triggering severe immune reactions or harmful off-target mutations. Conversely, plant scientists can edit cells in culture, screen thousands of regenerated plants for desired traits, and breed out unintended changes before release. While heritable germline editing in humans faces strict ethical bans, passing edits to offspring is the very goal of crop and livestock breeding. Regulatory timelines are also far shorter: human therapies require years of costly clinical trials, whereas many major agricultural nations regulate transgene-free edited crops like conventionally bred varieties, accelerating commercialization. Finally, economics and distribution favor agriculture. Human gene therapies often cost millions of dollars to treat one patient at a time for rare diseases, whereas a single edited seed line offering disease resistance or climate resilience can be multiplied cheaply and planted across millions of acres, benefiting billions of people worldwide.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Gene editing will likely reach far more people through farming than through medicine, mainly because the technical, regulatory and economic barriers are much lower in agriculture.

The technical problem is simpler. A plant breeder only needs to edit one cell or embryo, check the result, and multiply it through seeds or breeding. Human therapies have to deliver editing tools safely into enough of a patient's cells, which is still hard.

Regulation is lighter too. The US, Argentina, Brazil, Japan, India, England and others treat edited crops that carry no foreign DNA much like conventionally bred ones, and the EU is moving the same way. Medical therapies, by contrast, need years of costly clinical trials, and editing human embryos (changes that would be inherited) is widely prohibited.

The economics are very different. The first approved CRISPR therapy, Casgevy for sickle-cell disease, costs about $2 million per patient, so it reaches few people, mostly in rich countries. An improved seed can be cheaply copied and spread to millions of farmers.

Finally, the demand is large. Climate stress, crop disease and food security push for drought-tolerant, disease-resistant and more nutritious varieties. Edited products are already on the market or approved, including Japan's high-GABA tomato and disease-resistant pigs approved in the US.

In medicine, therapies must be safely delivered into specific tissues of living patients, where unintended mutations can be life-threatening. Developing them requires lengthy clinical trials and individualized treatment, often yielding costly therapies accessible to few patients.

In agriculture, scientists can edit plant cells in the lab, screen thousands of candidates to keep only those with precise edits, and discard the rest. Once a useful trait, such as drought tolerance or disease resistance, is established, it can be propagated cheaply through seeds and distributed to millions of farmers worldwide. Agricultural editing also avoids the strict ethical barriers around human germline modification and faces lighter regulation in many countries, especially when edits mimic natural mutations without adding foreign DNA. Together, these factors enable edited crops to scale globally far faster and more affordably than gene-edited medicines.
